# Phase 6 gate report: failure analysis, and the price of the only redesign the data points at

**Status: complete. The gate deliverables are done (tests, experiment, this report, commit).**

Phases 2 to 5 built the ladder and measured it. This phase does the two things the brief reserves
for the end: put the whole study on one frontier with the headline number the brief specified
(§B8), and explain the one result nobody's arithmetic predicted — that **four separate attacks on
bytes moved all failed to make decode faster**. Explaining it meant measuring what fixing it could
possibly be worth, before any of it was built.

The consolidated study is [`docs/FINDINGS.md`](../FINDINGS.md). This report is the gate for the work
that produced it.

## 1. The question this phase had to answer

Phase 5 closed with two candidate directions and a rule-8 note that choosing between them was the
owner's call. One of them — taking the residency decision off the host critical path — is a redesign
rather than a rung: it means keeping the top-K on the device and driving the gather from device
memory, so no layer has to synchronize to decide what it needs.

Building it first and measuring it second would have been the wrong order. So this phase prices it
first: **what is the largest speedup a perfect device-side residency decision could possibly
deliver?** If the answer had been 3×, the redesign would be the obvious next phase. §3 has it.

## 2. The instrument that did not work, and why it is kept

The obvious probe is the gap on the GPU stream between consecutive decoder layers: if the host has
to think between layers, the GPU should be starved and the gap should open up. It does open up, and
by nothing like enough.

| Condition | Budget | Inter-layer GPU gap, ms/token | Excess over the full cache, ms | Share of the saving it explains |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Full cache (rung 1) | 100% | 0.025 | 0.000 | - |
| CPU tier, int8 warm/cold (rung 8) | 25% | 0.459 | 0.435 | 7% |
| CPU tier, int8 warm/cold (rung 8) | 12.5% | 0.549 | 0.525 | 7% |
| CPU tier, int8 warm/cold (rung 8) | 6.25% | 0.252 | 0.227 | 3% |
| CPU tier, sync fetch (rung 6) | 25% | 0.502 | 0.478 | 7% |
| CPU tier, sync fetch (rung 6) | 12.5% | 0.374 | 0.350 | 5% |
| CPU tier, sync fetch (rung 6) | 6.25% | 0.557 | 0.532 | 7% |

The full cache's gap is 0.025 ms per token, and
the tier's excess over it is
0.23–0.53 ms —
a few percent of what §3 goes on to measure. The reason is structural rather than mysterious:
`select()` runs *inside* the attention module, so the stall it causes falls within a layer's span,
not between layers. An inter-layer probe cannot see it.

This is recorded rather than deleted because the negative result is the argument for the instrument
that replaced it. A reader who asks "why not just measure the bubble?" gets the number.

## 3. The replay ablation

Pass one decodes normally and records, for every layer at every step, which blocks the selection
chose. Pass two decodes the same prompt again driven by that record: the min/max bound never runs,
the host sync that brings the top-K indices back to the CPU never happens, and the blocks chosen,
the pairs fetched and the gathers performed stay identical. The difference in wall time is the
decision cost, isolated.

| Condition | Budget | Decode, ms/token | Replay, ms/token | Saved, ms | Ceiling | Rank+sync counted, ms | Saved - counted, ms | Pairs fetched | Replay token agreement |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Full cache (rung 1) | 100% | 21.72 | not measured | not measured | - | not measured | not measured | - | - |
| CPU tier, int8 warm/cold (rung 8) | 25% | 61.01 | 54.80 | 6.20 | **1.11x** | 6.64 | -0.44 | 45,133 = 45,133 | 99.3% |
| CPU tier, int8 warm/cold (rung 8) | 12.5% | 62.03 | 54.31 | 7.71 | **1.14x** | 6.64 | 1.07 | 64,488 = 64,488 | 99.3% |
| CPU tier, int8 warm/cold (rung 8) | 6.25% | 60.13 | 51.67 | 8.45 | **1.16x** | 6.86 | 1.60 | 57,245 = 57,245 | 98.5% |
| CPU tier, sync fetch (rung 6) | 25% | 52.29 | 45.40 | 6.88 | **1.15x** | 6.67 | 0.22 | 45,143 = 45,143 | 97.8% |
| CPU tier, sync fetch (rung 6) | 12.5% | 53.00 | 45.64 | 7.36 | **1.16x** | 6.67 | 0.69 | 64,442 = 64,442 | 98.5% |
| CPU tier, sync fetch (rung 6) | 6.25% | 52.60 | 45.18 | 7.42 | **1.16x** | 6.66 | 0.76 | 57,312 = 57,312 | 99.3% |

**The ceiling is 1.11–1.16×**,
or 6.2–8.5 ms
off a 52–62 ms
token. Two independent readings agree on it: the replay's measured saving lands within
1.6 ms of the rank-and-sync time that the
tier's own Phase 5 counters attribute to the same work, and those counters were not built to check
this.

### Why the ablation is trustworthy, in the terms it can fail

A ceiling is worth exactly as much as the evidence that the ablation changed only the decision:

| Guard | Why it matters | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Fetched pairs identical between passes | If replay moved different bytes it changed the work, and the difference would not be the decision cost | **True** at every condition |
| Token agreement reported, not asserted | The fast kernel is not bit-repeatable for single-query decode (Phase 1), so two identical passes can legitimately part on a near-tie | 97.8%–99.3%; a collapse would have meant something structural, a few late flips do not |
| Token sequence forced from the corpus | Without it one flipped token sends the passes down different paths, after which they seal different blocks and the comparison is meaningless | Both passes are teacher-forced on the same tokens |

Two attempts at this ablation were wrong before it was right, and **both were caught by the guards
rather than by inspection**. Greedy decode let the passes part on a near-tie, after which they
sealed different blocks; a dict-ordering slip let post-profiling counters overwrite the fetch count,
which made a clean ablation look broken. Each is a commit in the history, and each is the reason the
corresponding guard exists.

## 4. What the ceiling means, stated against the alternative

The replay still runs `admit`'s residency bookkeeping on the host, so it removes roughly half the
tier's host cost. A device-side design could attack the rest. If **all** of the tier's host select
time (20–28 ms
per token) vanished, decode would fall by
1.63–1.90×.
**That figure is arithmetic, not a measurement.** Phases 4 and 5 each found an arithmetic prediction
about this system to be wrong — prefetch that hid every copy was slower, and halving the bytes was
slower — so it is an optimistic bound and is quoted as one.

Even the optimistic bound does not change the decision. The full cache decodes a token in
21.7 ms; a tier with every scrap of host decision time
removed would still be near thirty. **A device-side residency decision closes part of the gap the
tier pays for its own mechanism, and never the gap to keeping KV in VRAM** at a context that still
fits there. The redesign is worth doing to make the memory win cheaper. It is not a route to beating
the full cache on latency, and this phase exists so that nobody spends a month discovering that.

## 5. The combined frontier

[`docs/FINDINGS.md`](../FINDINGS.md) puts all 8 rungs on one frontier and
answers brief §B8. Combining sweeps measured weeks apart in four separate gates is a claim, not a
formatting choice, so it is licensed by an explicit check:
17 conditions were measured in more than one phase, and the
largest accuracy disagreement across all of them is
**0.00 pp**. Accuracy is reproducible to the
last prompt. Decode speed is not — the same condition varies by up to
1.12× between phases, which is thermal and
run-to-run variation on a laptop, and is why every latency claim in the study carries a range.

The headline, in the brief's own terms: **no rung retains 99% of full-cache NIAH accuracy at any
budget below 100%**. The best any policy manages is
98.8% at a
75% budget. The brief asked for this
number because it is not gameable, and the honest answer on this task, at this context, with this
model, is *none*.
